title: Direct Upload of video content / large files
body:
This is a feature that we haven't tackled so far because of its relative complexity. Instead of building this, we've always suggested that users take advantage of existing video hosting platforms such as YouTube and Vimeo to upload their video content and then _embed_ them inside targets. The argument has been that these platforms have done an enormous amount of work into making the video upload / hosting easy, fast, accessible, and cheap.

However, there could be use-cases where this isn't practical, and where the user would prefer that these large files be managed directly by the LMS. In almost all cases, these large files appear to be videos, and the use is to stream video content.

The main "pain" driving this feature appears to be the inconvenience of uploading videos to another service - It would be really nice to be be able to use Pupilfirst to directly manage video content - something that is frequently an integral part of a course's content. To me, this looks like a good problem to solve.

However, another major driver appears to be to disallow students from sharing or downloading videos to their local systems - as a form of _Digital Rights Management_. The issue with this, is that whatever measures we take, there will always be ways around it, and to a technically capable user such measure are merely inconveniences. I'm unsure as to whether this is a direction we should even attempt to take.

### Options that I can see:

1. Build the feature-set in-house. This means building a direct-upload system (Rails [has good support for this, as of v6](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/active_storage_overview.html#direct-uploads)), **and also** the content-delivery side of it; I'm unfamiliar with the complexities of global streaming delivery of video - I'm sure there are plenty.
2. Integrate with a third-party service to manage video uploads and content delivery. For example: [Cloudflare Stream](https://www.cloudflare.com/products/cloudflare-stream).
3. Build both - i.e., build a direct upload system to handle generic large files (but only allow simple "downloads" of these), and seperately, integrate with a video upload & streaming service to handle hosting of streaming video content.

Options 2 & 3 look preferable to me, but IMHO, more research is required here.
author: Participant 1

comments.author: Participant 2
comments.body:
@harigopal , thanks for these ideas, very well captured and articulated , I digged in a bit to gather additional useful thoughts on option 2 & 3.

 [Cloudflare Stream](https://developers.cloudflare.com/stream/getting-started) seems to have some good reviews based on scalability, cost and functionality. It also disables downloading which is useful from _digital rights management_ perspective. Also, they use  [tus protocol](https://tus.io/) (recommended )  for resumable downloads  for files heavier than 200M

I checked  [GStreamer ](https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org/)which is an open source multi-media framework and i think this may have a huge learning curve , but maybe of interest in the future is that it supports  webRTC should we think in that direction in future. 

Also, I checked [ Amazon Elastic Transcoder ](https://aws.amazon.com/elastictranscoder/), which is not cheap at all and doesn't look all that straightforward.

Like you rightly mentioned, this feature seems to be ubiquitous  across most LMS and something worth looking into,but careful considerations be made to avoid unnecessary complications and especially it has to help the roadmap of pupilfirst.

comments.author: Participant 3
comments.body:
@adesokanayo @harigopal So I did further research. First, I don't think there's any good use-case to want to build both. For third-party integrations, there are a few other options. E.g. [Cloudinary](https://cloudinary.com), [Transloadit](https://transloadit.com). 

Cloudinary seems to be the most viable option in terms of;
- Cost: It has the most competitive pricing among all the options.
- Ease of Integration: It has first-hand integration with ActiveStorage - [here](https://cloudinary.com/documentation/rails_activestorage), unlike solutions like Transloadit & Cloudflare Streams where this integration will have to be custom-built.
- Ease of Backups: At competitive pricing, Cloudinary allows for easy backups to an S3 bucket, this can be achieved with the other options but will require some more work both in development time & job processing. There's great benefit in having all video files stored in an S3 bucket or Google Cloud Storage, this will enable us easily switch stream providers in the future, should in case we consider doing that. Unlike Cloudflare Streams where the uploads are directly managed by Cloudflare. 
- Video Player: Cloudinary comes with an already integrated video player.
- Globally Distributed CDN: Cloudinary comes with a globally distributed CDN ensuring top quality streaming availability.

Please let me know your thoughts.

comments.author: Participant 1
comments.body:
@Subomi I had a discussion about this with my team, and we're of the opinion that it would be best if the platform has as little involvement with the storage and handling of the video (and associated expenses) as possible. We propose an approach where school admins can upload videos directly to a Vimeo account that they own and manage.

### Proposed approach

1. Use [Vimeo's OAuth flow](https://developer.vimeo.com/api/authentication) to allow school admins to _connect_ their own Vimeo account to the school.
2. On the target content editor, if a Vimeo account is connected, enable a new _Video_ content block type.
3. When the block-type is selected, ask the user to pick a video file.
4. Send details of the video, including its byte-size to the Rails server.
5. At the server, use the video file details to [create a video at Vimeo](https://developer.vimeo.com/api/upload/videos#resumable-approach) - make sure to set `privacy.embed` to the school's known FQDN-s, and then return the `upload_link` and `uri` that was returned by Vimeo.
6. At the client, use the `upload_link` and an appropriate brower-based TUS library to upload the video file.
7. Once upload is completed and verified, use the `uri` that was supplied by Vimeo earlier with the existing embed flow to embed the Vimeo link.

### Why this approach?

1. This approach seems to involve the least amount of work. 😁 
2. School administrators retain full ownership of video content.
3. Vimeo's privacy controls ensure that videos can be played only via the school.
4. Moving to another service or platform is possible since Vimeo's API allows downloads of original content.

One aspect of this that can be seen as a disadvantage is that school admins need to get a subscription to _another_ service to make the `privacy.embed` feature work. However, the cheapest plan from Vimeo will allow this to work, and we think it's reasonably priced - it begins at an affordable USD 12 p/m or 84 p/y.

This flow should still work, even without a paid plan - I think that the `privacy.embed` feature would be the only thing that'd have to be left out if the connected account is on the _free_ tier.

@pupilfirst/developers Note.

comments.author: Participant 3
comments.body:
@harigopal Hmm... Interesting approach. I agree that we should have has little as possible involvement with the storage and handling of the video as much as possible. It was the same reason I opted for the Cloudinary solution. The flow you described is [Direct Uploads](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/active_storage_overview.html#direct-uploads).

It is the exact same thing with Cloudinary's approach. The difference is the Cloudinary as implemented the service class for `ActiveStorage::Service` base class and we'd have to implement the service class for Vimeo. I don't think this _should_ be a problem though. 

I guess the other thing I didn't factor in is who bears the cost 🤔 with this approach obviously the cost shifts to the school admins vs. the platform. I think we should also take into consideration how much we spend to offer this solution vs. how much school admins will have to pay using Vimeo to use this feature i.e. Cloudinary Plus is $89/m which means $1068/yr for all users. vs. $84/yr for each user using Vimeo, 13 users doing this equals the same cost. But for a start, I think $7 is fair enough. 👍 

Also, the privacy features Vimeo provides is also a big win in terms of what we should handle vs. what should be handled for us.  I'd start looking into the exact implementations for `ActiveStorage::Service` for Vimeo and feedback here.

comments.author: Participant 1
comments.body:
@Subomi There should be no ActiveStorage involvement in the flow that I described. In fact, this should involve zero new entries being added to the database (other than the final embed block).

Videos are being directly uploaded to Vimeo from the browser, and our server has no record of the file itself. Please go through the flow I described again - you'll note that the only time the server gets involved is to use the stored API token to generate the upload URL (`upload_link`) and the final Vimeo URL (`uri`); after that it's upto the client to actually _put_ the file on Vimeo, and then instruct the server to embed the `uri`.

> Cloudinary Plus is $89/m which means $1068/yr for all users. vs. $84/yr for each user using Vimeo

Yeah, we had similar discussions as well, and we decided that the math isn't quite so straight-forward. i.e, $1068/yr _for all users_...

Cloudinary has **three** different limits on their plan - and all clients aren't going to use the video upload feature equally. The only _fair_ way to split this kind of service for end users would be to pass on a fraction of these limits down to them (in such a way that it makes fiscal sense). However, the scary part of that is having to keep track of all of the limits that Cloudinary imposes on a per resource, or per-client basis - storage, viewing bandwidth, and video processing seconds. Except for the first (which is already tracked by ActiveStorage), I couldn't even figure out a way to _get_ that info via their API. Taking this route would definitely involve a _lot_ of additional work that doesn't actually help the _feature_ itself.

comments.author: Participant 2
comments.body:
From a User Experience  standpoint , this would mean to be able to use this feature, you must also own a Vimeo account  and to enjoy privacy , it has to be a paid plan. How about the platform leveraging a single Vimeo account instead of every school having their own account ?

This will be similar to the way we use s3 today. The platform has a single s3 instance rather than asking schools to connect to their individual s3 instances, this make the value proposition better  IMO.

comments.author: Participant 3
comments.body:
@harigopal I understand the flow better now. To break it down further flowing is required: 

Vimeo OAuth:
- We'd be using the auth code for our use case. 
- create `getVimeoOauthLink` query to get the OAuth link.
- create OAuth redirect uri to receive auth code to retrieve the `access_token`

Video Upload:
- Add Video Content Block Type inside the target content editor, `ContentBlock` model.
- On selecting a video.
   - Create a `createVideoContent` mutation that returns `upload_link` and `uri`. Also, create the content block as an `embed` type.
   - Start uploading with `tus` library. 

Video Download: 
- The Vimeo player already includes this feature for all paid Vimeo accounts. 
- create `toggleVideoDownloadable` mutation If the video should not be downloadable. I don't think it is a good UX to require the user to configure this in their Vimeo account. This can/should be controlled by an icon by the side.

Questions:
- I'm not sure what `video_embed` column is used for in the targets table.

@adesokanayo I'm not quite sure about a single Vimeo account because we're still hit with having to do the math to split the costs across all users and the work (code) of tracking usage per user obviously more work than we want to do on this feature now. 🤔

comments.author: Participant 1
comments.body:
> From a User Experience standpoint , this would mean to be able to use this feature, you must also own a Vimeo account and to enjoy privacy , it has to be a paid plan.

@adesokanayo Correct. This isn't the _best_ option from a user-experience standpoint. What we're doing here is simply the most _reasonable_ / _achievable_ option that solves the biggest pain-points: namely: 1) the inability to upload videos straight from the LMS interface and 2) the inability to lock down the videos such that they can be played only on the LMS website.

The inconvenience of having to sign-up for a second service (Vimeo) remains - however this sign-up and set-up of the Vimeo account should be a one-time activity.

> How about the platform leveraging a single Vimeo account instead of every school having their own account ? This will be similar to the way we use s3 today.

Unfortunately, AWS S3 and Vimeo are very different kinds of services. Vimeo serves the end-user directly, whereas AWS's services are targeted towards developers who build applications for _their own_ clients. Vimeo simply isn't _meant_ to be used in such a fashion, and so doesn't provide the tooling or API-s necessary for this kind of _"shared"_ use.

In fact, if we ever decide to _manage_ the storage of video files in-house, I would certainly prefer to use AWS's stack of services over trying to use Vimeo, or probably even Cloudinary.

@Subomi Your OAuth flow, and the changes to the LMS look and sound _about_ right. However, I think that it would be easier to discuss the specifics of how this can be implemented, over on Discord. I'll ping you there.
